one_t.title: One-sample t-test
one_t.summary: Estimate how far a process mean is from a specified target.
one_t.why: You have one set of independent numerical measurements and want to compare its population mean with a fixed reference value.

setup.title: Assign the measurement
setup.text: Move your numerical measurement to Variables. Each row should represent one independent sampled unit; do not enter only the sample mean.

setup.title: Enter the target
setup.text: Set Test value to the specified target. Retain Student under Tests. Choose a one-sided alternative only when the direction was chosen before examining the results.

setup.title: Request useful output
setup.text: Select Location estimate and its Confidence interval, Descriptives, and a raincloud or Q-Q plot. Report the difference in the original measurement units.

setup.title: Optional Bayesian analysis
setup.text: T-Tests > Bayesian > One Sample T-Test provides Bayes factors and posterior estimates. Specify and examine the prior; a Bayes factor for a point null addresses a different question from practical equivalence.

columns.name: Item
columns.description: One identifier per independently sampled package.

columns.name: FillWeight
columns.description: Measured package mass in grams; the example target is 500 g.

checks: Check how the sample was collected. Consecutive, autocorrelated readings or many measurements from the same batch may require a model that represents that dependence.
Inspect the measurement distribution and unusual values, especially with a small sample. A normality-test p-value alone should not choose the analysis.
The target is an external reference, not a second sample mean estimated with uncertainty.
A test of the mean does not establish that individual items meet specification limits. A nonsignificant result does not establish equivalence.
report: Sample size, mean, standard deviation, target and estimated mean difference with a confidence interval.
The test, alternative hypothesis and p-value; interpret the magnitude in the context of an engineering tolerance.
How units were sampled and any evidence of dependence, drift or influential measurements.

example.title: Is the average fill on target?
example.story: A packaging line has a nominal fill of 500 g. Independent sampled packages are weighed to estimate the difference between the process mean and that target.
instructions: Move FillWeight to Variables and enter 500 as Test value.
Request the location estimate, its confidence interval and Descriptives.
For the question 'close enough to 500 g', use the equivalence route and a prespecified acceptable deviation.

related.label: Show the mean is close enough to the target

ind_t.title: Independent-samples t-test · Welch
ind_t.summary: Compare the means of two groups of independently sampled units.
ind_t.why: Each unit belongs to one group, the outcome is numerical, and your question concerns a difference in population means. Welch's test allows the group variances to differ.

setup.title: Use one measurement column
setup.text: Move Measurement to Dependent Variables and Group to Grouping Variable. Group must contain exactly two levels.

setup.title: Select Welch
setup.text: Select Welch under Tests. Deselect Student if you want a single primary test. You do not need a preliminary variance test to justify using Welch.

setup.title: Show the size of the difference
setup.text: Request Location parameter and its Confidence interval, Descriptives, and raincloud plots. Check which group is subtracted from which.

setup.title: Optional Bayesian analysis
setup.text: The Bayesian section of T-Tests includes an independent-samples test. Its standard model is not simply Welch's test with a Bayes factor; examine the model assumptions and prior before using it.

columns.name: Part
columns.description: One identifier per independently sampled part.

columns.name: Group
columns.description: Two process labels, A and B.

checks: These are different units in the two groups. If the same parts were measured twice, choose the paired route.
Repeated readings from the same part, batch or machine are not automatically independent replicates.
Inspect outliers and each group's distribution. Welch addresses unequal variances, not severe dependence or all small-sample distribution problems.
An ordinary difference test cannot establish that two processes are practically equivalent.
report: Group sample sizes, means and standard deviations; the mean difference and its confidence interval in millimetres.
Welch's t statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value and the prespecified alternative.
Whether the difference is large enough to matter for the process, separate from statistical significance.

example.title: Do two suppliers produce different dimensions?
example.story: Independent parts from suppliers A and B are measured. The engineering question concerns their average dimension, not whether their variances or individual defect rates are equal.
instructions: Set Group to Nominal and Measurement to Scale.
Assign Measurement and Group, then select Welch.
Inspect the confidence interval for the mean difference and compare it with a meaningful engineering difference.

related.label: The same units were measured twice

paired_t.title: Paired-samples t-test
paired_t.summary: Estimate the mean change within matched units.
paired_t.why: Each before measurement has a meaningful after measurement from the same unit or a prespecified matched partner. The analysis uses the differences within those pairs.

setup.title: Keep each pair on one row
setup.text: Arrange Before and After in separate numerical columns. Each row represents one matched pair. Keep Part as an identifier.

setup.title: Define the pair
setup.text: Move Before and After into one row in Variable Pairs and retain Student under Tests. The column order defines the sign of the difference.

setup.title: Inspect differences
setup.text: Request Location parameter, its Confidence interval and Descriptives. Use Raincloud difference plots or the Q-Q plot to inspect the within-pair differences.

setup.title: Optional Bayesian analysis
setup.text: T-Tests > Bayesian > Paired Samples T-Test provides a Bayes factor and posterior estimates for the standardized within-pair effect. Examine the prior and distinguish evidence about zero change from practical equivalence.

columns.name: Part
columns.description: Identifies the work item or matched pair.

columns.name: Before
columns.description: Cycle time before a workflow change, in seconds.

columns.name: After
columns.description: Cycle time after the change for the matching work item, in seconds.

checks: The matching must reflect the design; similar row numbers or equal sample sizes do not create genuine pairs.
Independent pairs are required. Additional repeats within a part or batch need a model that represents that structure.
For a small sample, inspect the distribution of the differences. Separate normality tests on Before and After do not assess the paired-test assumption.
Before–after data can be affected by time trends, learning or other simultaneous changes. Pairing alone does not establish a causal effect.
report: Number of complete pairs and the mean difference with a confidence interval in seconds.
State the subtraction order, such as Before minus After, and the selected alternative.
Describe matching, missing pairs and any factors that could explain the change.

example.title: Did a workflow change reduce cycle time?
example.story: Each work item has a cycle-time measurement before and after a change. Matching removes much of the variation caused by some items inherently taking longer.
instructions: Create the pair Before–After in Variable Pairs.
Inspect the differences and their confidence interval.
A positive Before minus After estimate means the after measurements were faster.

related.label: Show the average change is acceptably small
The same units have three or more measurements

one_anova.title: One-way ANOVA · Welch option
one_anova.summary: Compare a numerical outcome across three or more independent groups.
one_anova.why: You have one grouping factor and independent units in its groups. An ANOVA assesses whether all population means are equal; follow-up comparisons identify the differences of interest.

setup.title: Assign the outcome and group
setup.text: Move Measurement to Dependent Variable and Group to Fixed Factors. For this route, use one grouping factor.

setup.title: Choose the variance assumption
setup.text: Under Assumption Checks > Homogeneity corrections, select Welch for a one-way comparison that allows unequal variances. The standard ANOVA is appropriate when a common residual variance is defensible.

setup.title: Plan the follow-up comparisons
setup.text: In Post Hoc Tests, assign Group. Games-Howell accommodates unequal group variances. For the standard equal-variance model, Tukey compares all pairs and Dunnett compares groups with a reference.

setup.title: Inspect the data and report uncertainty
setup.text: Request descriptives, plots and suitable intervals. Avoid reporting only the overall p-value. A Bayesian ANOVA is also available in ANOVA > Bayesian, with its own model and prior assumptions.

columns.name: Group
columns.description: Process or machine labels A, B and C.

checks: The same part must not contribute measurements to multiple groups in this independent-groups route.
Welch's correction here is for a one-way design. Multiple experimental factors and their interactions require the appropriate factorial model.
Inspect residuals, group distributions and influential values; do not let a single normality or variance test mechanically choose the method.
Use planned contrasts or adjust for multiple comparisons. Separate unadjusted t-tests inflate false-positive risk.
report: Group sample sizes, means and spreads, and the overall test with its variance assumption.
The comparisons that matter operationally, with effect estimates, intervals and the multiplicity adjustment.
Whether observed differences exceed a prespecified practically relevant amount.

example.title: Compare three production machines
example.story: Different parts are sampled from machines A, B and C. The goal is to locate differences in average part dimension while allowing the machines to have different variability.
instructions: Assign Measurement as Dependent Variable and Group as Fixed Factors.
Select Welch under Homogeneity corrections.
If comparing all pairs, request Games-Howell and interpret the differences in millimetres.

related.label: Measurements are repeated on the same units

rm_anova.title: Repeated-measures ANOVA
rm_anova.summary: Compare three or more conditions measured on the same units.
rm_anova.why: The same units are observed under several conditions. The analysis represents their shared identity instead of treating every measurement as independent.

setup.title: Use one row per unit
setup.text: Place the measurements from each condition in separate columns, such as Setting_A, Setting_B and Setting_C. Keep Part as an identifier.

setup.title: Define the repeated factor
setup.text: Create a repeated-measures factor named Setting with three levels. Assign the three measurement columns to their matching Repeated Measures Cells.

setup.title: Assess the repeated-measures assumptions
setup.text: Request the sphericity test and sphericity corrections. With more than two levels, report an appropriate correction, such as Greenhouse–Geisser, when the uncorrected assumption is not defensible.

setup.title: Compare the relevant conditions
setup.text: Request descriptive plots and planned or adjusted follow-up comparisons. A Bayesian repeated-measures analysis is also available under ANOVA > Bayesian; check its model and prior assumptions.

columns.name: Part
columns.description: The same physical unit across all three conditions.

columns.name: Setting_A
columns.description: Measurement under setting A, in millimetres.

columns.name: Setting_B
columns.description: Measurement under setting B, in millimetres.

columns.name: Setting_C
columns.description: Measurement under setting C, in millimetres.

checks: Units should be independent of one another even though measurements within a unit are related.
Randomize or counterbalance condition order when possible; setting effects can otherwise be confounded with time or carry-over.
Unbalanced repeats, many missing measurements, nested batches or complex time dependence may require a mixed model instead.
A significant overall test says some mean differs. It does not identify which conditions or whether the differences matter in practice.
report: The number of complete units, condition means and planned or adjusted comparisons.
The repeated factor, sphericity correction and associated test results.
Measurement order, missing-data handling and the practical magnitude of differences.

example.title: Compare three settings on the same parts
example.story: Each part is measured under settings A, B and C. A row contains all three measurements from the same part.
instructions: Create Setting with three levels and assign Setting_A, Setting_B and Setting_C to the matching cells.
Inspect sphericity corrections and a plot of the condition means.
Use adjusted pairwise comparisons when several setting comparisons are of interest.

eq_one.title: One-sample equivalence test
eq_one.summary: Assess whether a process mean is close enough to its target.
eq_one.why: Your claim concerns a practically acceptable deviation from a target. An equivalence test directly evaluates whether the mean difference lies inside prespecified bounds.

setup.title: Activate the module
setup.text: Enable Equivalence T-Tests in JASP's module selector if it is not already visible. Choose its Classical One Sample T-Test.

setup.title: Specify the measurement and target
setup.text: Assign FillWeight_deviation_g = FillWeight − 500 to Variables and enter Test value 0.

setup.title: Set meaningful bounds
setup.text: Under Equivalence Region, choose Bounds specification in: Raw. Enter bounds for the deviation from the target, for example −1 to +1 g. Choose these bounds before inspecting the data.

setup.title: Read both one-sided tests
setup.text: At alpha 0.05, equivalence requires both bound tests to reject non-equivalence; equivalently, the relevant 90% confidence interval must lie entirely within the bounds. Request the Equivalence bounds plot.

setup.title: Colleague preview — 7 November 2026
setup.text: Preserve all 60 measurements and derive FillWeight_deviation_g = FillWeight − 500. Test against 0 with raw bounds −1/+1 g, alpha .05. This avoids the ignored nonzero-reference problem. Mean deviation .3776667 g, 90% CI [−.0679096,.8232429]. Both tests reject: lower-bound hypothesis t=5.166813, p=.000001480; upper-bound hypothesis t=−2.334004, p=.0115105. The current lower/upper test-row labels are interchanged; interpret the hypotheses and interval, not those row labels.

checks: Bounds describe an acceptable difference in the process mean. They are not the specification limits for individual products.
Use raw engineering units when those define acceptability. Do not leave the software's default equivalence bounds without justification.
The independent-measurement and distribution requirements of a one-sample mean analysis still apply.
Failure to establish equivalence can reflect an imprecise sample; it does not by itself establish a practically important difference.

Preserve all 60 measurements and derive FillWeight_deviation_g = FillWeight − 500. Test against 0 with raw bounds −1/+1 g, alpha .05. This avoids the ignored nonzero-reference problem. Mean deviation .3776667 g, 90% CI [−.0679096,.8232429]. Both tests reject: lower-bound hypothesis t=5.166813, p=.000001480; upper-bound hypothesis t=−2.334004, p=.0115105. The current lower/upper test-row labels are interchanged; interpret the hypotheses and interval, not those row labels.
report: The target, equivalence bounds, units and engineering justification selected before analysis.
The estimated deviation, relevant confidence interval, alpha level and both one-sided test results.
State whether equivalence was established, with separate assessment of process spread and individual conformance.

example.title: Is mean fill within 1 g of the target?
example.story: Suppose engineering requirements define an acceptable mean deviation of at most 1 g from a 500 g target. This is a question about the mean; the allowable range for individual packages is a separate requirement.
instructions: Assign FillWeight_deviation_g and set Test value to 0.
Choose Raw bounds −1/+1 g, alpha .05, and the equivalence plot.
Use the verified interval and both one-sided hypotheses; do not infer the hypothesis from the interchanged row labels.

related.label: Test for a difference from the target

eq_ind.title: Equivalence test for independent groups
eq_ind.summary: Assess whether two independent process means are close enough for a defined purpose.
eq_ind.why: You want positive evidence that the difference in two population means lies within an engineering tolerance, rather than relying on a nonsignificant ordinary t-test.

setup.title: Assign the outcome and group
setup.text: Enable Equivalence T-Tests if needed. Move Measurement to Dependent Variables and Group to Grouping Variable.

setup.title: Choose Welch
setup.text: Select Welch under Tests when using a model that allows unequal group variances. Confirm the group order used for the mean difference.

setup.title: Enter the acceptance region
setup.text: Set Bounds specification in to Raw and enter the prespecified acceptable mean difference, for example −0.05 to +0.05 mm.

setup.title: Inspect the equivalence interval
setup.text: Request Descriptives and the Equivalence bounds plot. With alpha 0.05, both one-sided tests must reject, which corresponds to the 90% interval lying entirely within the two bounds.

columns.name: Group
columns.description: Process A or B; exactly two groups.

checks: Choose bounds from the application before inspecting the estimated difference. The example's ±0.05 mm is an illustrative tolerance.
Equality of means does not ensure equality of variances, tail risks or overall process capability.
Independent samples are required. Use the paired equivalence route for the same units measured twice.
A result may be statistically different from zero and practically equivalent at the same time. An inconclusive result may establish neither.
report: Both group sample sizes and the estimated mean difference with its equivalence confidence interval.
The bounds in raw units, justification, alpha level and both one-sided test results.
Whether equivalence of the means was established, and what additional process characteristics still require assessment.

example.title: Can a replacement supplier match the mean dimension?
example.story: Before the study, engineering specifies that a replacement supplier's mean dimension may differ by at most 0.05 mm from the existing supplier. Different parts are sampled from the two suppliers.
instructions: Assign Measurement and Group, select Welch and set Raw bounds to −0.05 and +0.05.
Read the equivalence interval and both bound tests.
Assess variation and defect rates separately before making a broader interchangeability claim.

related.label: The same units were measured twice

eq_paired.title: Paired equivalence test
eq_paired.summary: Assess whether the average within-pair difference is acceptably small.
eq_paired.why: Two measurements are genuinely paired and you have a prespecified acceptable range for their population mean difference.

setup.title: Keep matching measurements together
setup.text: Use one row per pair and separate Before and After columns. Enable Equivalence T-Tests if needed.

setup.title: Assign the pair
setup.text: Move Before and After into Variable Pairs. Check the subtraction order, especially for asymmetric acceptance bounds.

setup.title: Specify the allowable difference
setup.text: Set Bounds specification in to Raw and enter the prespecified interval for the mean difference, for example −1 to +1 second.

setup.title: Request the equivalence plot
setup.text: At alpha 0.05, equivalence requires the relevant 90% interval to lie wholly within the bounds and both one-sided tests to reject non-equivalence.

columns.name: After
columns.description: Matching second cycle-time measurement in seconds.

checks: Matching must come from the study design, and different pairs should be independent.
Inspect within-pair differences and their outliers; do not assess the paired model solely from the two separate marginal distributions.
Equivalence of average measurement bias does not establish agreement for individual measurements. A measurement-system study may be needed for interchangeability.
Specify bounds before examining the data and distinguish an inconclusive result from established equivalence.
report: Number of complete pairs, subtraction order, mean difference and equivalence confidence interval.
Prespecified bounds in seconds, alpha level and both one-sided test results.
The exact scope of the conclusion: the average paired difference, not every individual difference.

example.title: Does the change preserve mean cycle time?
example.story: Suppose a workflow change is acceptable only if its average cycle-time change remains within ±1 second. The same work items are measured before and after.
instructions: Assign Before–After as a pair and choose Raw bounds from −1 to +1.
Read the equivalence plot; the paired differences, not the two separate means, determine precision.
The example tolerance illustrates setup and should be replaced by a justified requirement in a real study.

binomial.title: Binomial test
binomial.summary: Compare one pass/fail probability with a specified benchmark.
binomial.why: Each independent item has a binary outcome, and you want to estimate or test the probability of one defined event such as failure.

setup.title: Use item-level outcomes
setup.text: Use one row per inspected item with a nominal Result column containing Pass or Fail. Move Result to Variables. Do not enter the lot percentages as binary observations.

setup.title: Enter the benchmark probability
setup.text: Set Test value to the probability benchmark for the event you will interpret, for example 0.05 for a 5% failure rate. Read the output row for Fail.

setup.title: Choose direction and uncertainty
setup.text: Choose the prespecified alternative and request a confidence interval. A claim that failure probability is below a maximum needs evidence in that direction; failure to reject equality is insufficient.

setup.title: Optional Bayesian analysis
setup.text: Frequencies > Bayesian > Binomial Test provides evidence and estimation under a specified prior. Select the event and prior deliberately; do not confuse the pass probability with the failure probability.

columns.name: Result
columns.description: Exactly one of Pass or Fail for each item.

checks: Each item contributes one binary classification. Multiple defects on the same item are a different kind of count.
The total number inspected is needed. A count of failures alone does not determine a failure proportion.
The simple binomial model assumes independent items with a common probability. Clustering by lot or changes over time may require a different analysis.
Choose the event, benchmark and direction before looking at the observed rate. For ongoing monitoring, use an appropriate attribute control chart.
report: Number of failures and total inspected, observed failure proportion and its uncertainty interval.
The benchmark probability, event definition, alternative and selected test result.
Whether the evidence supports the operational claim and whether the inspection sample represents the intended process.

example.title: Assess a failure-rate benchmark
example.story: Each inspected component is recorded as Pass or Fail. The team wants to assess its failure probability against a 5% benchmark.
instructions: Move Result to Variables and enter 0.05 as Test value.
Request a confidence interval and interpret the Fail row.
Use a prespecified lower alternative only if the intended claim is that the failure probability is below 5%.

related.label: Compare pass/fail rates between independent groups

contingency.title: Contingency tables · independent groups
contingency.summary: Compare categorical outcomes between independent groups.
contingency.why: You want to determine whether the distribution of outcomes, such as Pass and Fail, is associated with a grouping variable such as supplier.

setup.title: Choose the data layout
setup.text: For individual records, use one row per item with Supplier and Result. For summarized records, use one row per Supplier × Result combination and a Count column.

setup.title: Assign rows, columns and counts
setup.text: Move Supplier to Rows and Result to Columns. For summarized data only, move Count to Counts; leave Counts empty for individual records.

setup.title: Inspect proportions and expected counts
setup.text: Request row percentages and expected cell counts. Pearson's chi-squared test is the standard association test when the approximation is adequate.

setup.title: Handle a sparse 2 × 2 table
setup.text: For two groups and two outcomes, request Odds ratio (2x2 only) to obtain Fisher's exact test and an effect interval. The interface also offers a log-odds display; label whichever scale you report.

columns.name: Supplier
columns.description: Independent groups; suppliers A, B and C in the example.

columns.name: Result
columns.description: Outcome category; Pass/Fail in the example.

columns.name: Count
columns.description: Nonnegative integer number of items in this Supplier × Result combination; use only for summarized records.

checks: Different groups must contain independent items. Paired pass/fail measurements require a paired categorical analysis, not the ordinary independence test.
Enter counts, not rounded percentages. Keep the denominators and all outcome categories.
For sparse larger tables, Pearson's approximation may be poor. A 2 × 2 Fisher test is not a general solution for every larger design.
An association need not be causal: suppliers may differ in product mix, inspection or other factors. Logistic regression can incorporate measured predictors.
report: The category counts and within-group proportions, with the relevant denominators.
The chosen test and effect estimate with an interval; specify event coding and reference group.
The practical difference in quality and any confounding or sampling limitations.

example.title: Compare three suppliers’ nonconforming proportions
example.story: Independent deliveries from suppliers A, B and C are inspected. Counts are summarized into six supplier-by-result rows.
instructions: Assign Supplier to Rows, Result to Columns and Count to Counts.
Request row percentages and expected counts.
This is a 3 × 2 table. Examine expected counts before interpreting Pearson’s chi-squared test; the 2 × 2 Fisher option does not apply to the full table.

related.label: Compare one failure rate with a benchmark

doe_factorial.title: Create a factorial design
doe_factorial.summary: Plan runs to study several factors and their interactions.
doe_factorial.why: You want to learn which controllable factors affect a response. A factorial design varies factors together so their main effects and interactions can be studied.

setup.title: Define the experiment
setup.text: Specify the response, experimental unit, feasible factor ranges and minimum relevant effects before selecting a design. Worksheet creation does not require an existing dataset.

setup.title: Choose factors and design type
setup.text: Enter Number of factors, names and levels. Choose a 2-level factorial design for low/high factors or General full factorial when factors need more levels.

setup.title: Select a design row
setup.text: Click a suitable candidate in the Design Table and enable Display design. Without selecting a candidate, an empty result can look like the analysis is not working.

setup.title: Plan replication and restrictions
setup.text: Set replications, blocks and center points as justified by the study. Inspect Alias structure for fractional designs. Use a reproducible seed and the randomized run order.

setup.title: Export and collect responses
setup.text: Choose the CSV destination and Export design. Run the experiment in its planned order, record the response alongside factor settings, then use Analyse Design.

setup.title: Colleague preview — 7 November 2026
setup.text: Create one unreplicated full 2³ design: eight randomized runs, Temperature 160/180 °C, Pressure 2/4 bar, Speed 40/60 rpm, one block (no blocking restriction), no center points, seed 261107. This avoids unwanted replicate blocks. All eight combinations occur once. Response is blank until data collection; replication-based error estimation is unavailable. The original completed 16-run example is preserved separately for Analyse Design.

checks: A fractional design can confound effects. Check its resolution and alias structure against the interactions that matter.
Repeated measurements of one experimental run are not independent run replications.
For continuous factors, center points can help reveal curvature, but a two-level design with centers does not separately estimate every quadratic effect.

Hard-to-change factors require restricted randomization and an analysis with the correct error structure. JASP offers split-plot worksheet creation, but the ordinary factorial analysis should not be assumed to solve every split-plot design.
Blocks represent planned nuisance variation such as day or raw-material batch. Decide how blocking and randomization will work before collecting data.

Create one unreplicated full 2³ design: eight randomized runs, Temperature 160/180 °C, Pressure 2/4 bar, Speed 40/60 rpm, one block (no blocking restriction), no center points, seed 261107. This avoids unwanted replicate blocks. All eight combinations occur once. Response is blank until data collection; replication-based error estimation is unavailable. The original completed 16-run example is preserved separately for Analyse Design.
report: Factor definitions, natural levels, response, run order, independent replications and blocking.
Full or fractional design, alias structure, center points and design-selection rationale.
Execution deviations and the planned model and follow-up confirmation runs.

example.title: Create an eight-run factorial preview
example.story: Synthetic teaching design generated natively in JASP with seed 261107; eight randomized runs and no collected responses.
instructions: Create three two-level factors: Temperature 160/180, Pressure 2/4, Speed 40/60.
Select the full 2³ candidate; use one replicate, one block, zero centers, randomization and seed 261107. Enable Display design.
Export the eight-run worksheet. Keep Response blank until collection; this design has no replication-based pure-error estimate.
The separate factorial example contains the original 16 completed runs for Analyse Design.

doe_surface.title: Create a response-surface design
doe_surface.summary: Plan an experiment that can model curvature and locate useful operating settings.
doe_surface.why: The important continuous factors are sufficiently well understood to investigate curvature and optimize a response within a chosen operating region.

setup.title: Define a feasible operating region
setup.text: Choose continuous factors, their practical ranges and the response goal. No existing dataset is required to create the worksheet.

setup.title: Choose the design
setup.text: Select Central composite design or Box-Behnken design. In the verified interface, central composite designs support two or more continuous factors; Box-Behnken starts at three.

setup.title: Select a candidate row
setup.text: Click a candidate in the Design Table and enable Display design. Define factor names and low/high levels, then inspect all proposed runs.

setup.title: Check axial points and centers
setup.text: For a central composite design, Alpha controls axial distances in coded units. Face centred uses axial points at the low/high limits; other choices can extend beyond the factorial low/high settings. Set center points, replicates and seed deliberately.

setup.title: Export, collect and analyse
setup.text: Export the design CSV, follow the planned execution order and record responses. Then choose Analyse Design > Response surface design, fit an appropriate quadratic model and inspect contour plots and residuals.

columns.name: Yield
columns.description: Measured continuous yield response in percent, away from its bounds in this example.

checks: Verify every proposed setting is feasible. In a central composite design, axial points can lie outside the factorial cube.
Center-point repetitions should be genuine independent experimental runs. They help assess pure error and curvature.
Keep the intended factorial low/high settings for analysis. Automatic low/high detection can mistake axial values for factorial levels; specify the original levels manually when necessary.
A fitted optimum is a prediction within a model. Check residuals, keep optimization within justified bounds and confirm promising settings in new runs.
For hard-to-change factors, constraints or noncontinuous responses, review whether the design and analysis represent the experiment correctly.
report: Design type, factor ranges, axial distance, center points, replication, blocks and run order.
The fitted model, residual checks and response surface within the investigated region.
Proposed settings and the results of independent confirmation runs.

example.title: Find a useful temperature and processing time
example.story: A team explores curvature in yield across temperatures of 160–180 °C and processing times of 20–40 minutes. The synthetic two-factor face-centred central composite design has 13 randomized runs: four corners, four axial points and five independent center runs at 170 °C and 30 minutes.
instructions: For a new design, choose Central composite design, two continuous factors and Face centred Alpha; select a design row and Display design.
For the example CSV, use Analyse Design > Response surface design with Yield as the response and Temperature and Time as continuous factors.
Select a Full quadratic model, inspect residuals, and request a contour or surface plot.

doe_analyze.title: Analyse a designed experiment
doe_analyze.summary: Fit the model corresponding to your factorial or response-surface experiment.
doe_analyze.why: You have completed experimental runs with controlled factor settings and measured responses. The analysis must preserve the design's factors, interactions, coding and blocking.

setup.title: Select the design type
setup.text: Open the completed dataset and choose Factorial design or Response surface design, matching the experiment that was actually run.

setup.title: Assign response and factors
setup.text: Place outcomes in Responses, quantitative factors in Continuous factors and categorical factors in Discrete factors. Assign a planned blocking variable to Blocks where appropriate.

setup.title: Verify levels and model terms
setup.text: Check Factor levels, particularly low/high settings in a response-surface design. Specify the model from the design and scientific question. Include interactions when estimable; Full quadratic is available for response-surface designs.

setup.title: Inspect the model
setup.text: Request the regression equation, relevant effect plots and Residuals four-in-one plot. Keep rows in actual execution order for residuals versus run order. Choose coded or natural units deliberately.

setup.title: Optimize after checking fit
setup.text: For optimization, include responses in Response optimizer, set Maximize, Minimize or Target goals and appropriate bounds, then request Show optimal solution. Validate promising settings with new experimental runs.

columns.name: Run
columns.description: Execution order; keep rows in this order when assessing drift.

columns.name: Strength
columns.description: Response in MPa for the factorial example.

checks: Respect aliasing and estimability. A saturated or unreplicated design may leave no independent residual-error estimate for ordinary tests.
An interaction means one factor's effect depends on another factor. Retain a coherent model hierarchy when interpreting it.
Restricted randomization, split plots and nested experimental units can require multiple error terms. Do not assume the ordinary model is valid for every such design.
For two-level coded factors, an effect and a regression coefficient can differ by a scaling factor. Check output definitions before interpreting apparent inconsistencies.
Automatic model selection and optimization can overstate performance. Evaluate residuals and confirm predictions with new runs.
report: Experimental design, response, factor coding, block structure and fitted model terms.
Effects with uncertainty, interactions, residual diagnostics and limits from aliasing or sample size.
Any proposed settings, the region over which predictions are supported and confirmation-run results.

example.title: Analyse a replicated bond-strength experiment
example.story: The synthetic dataset contains 16 randomized runs: two independent replicates of a 2³ experiment using temperature 160/180 °C, pressure 2/4 bar and speed 40/60 rpm. The response is bond strength in MPa.
instructions: Choose Factorial design and assign Strength to Responses.
Assign Temperature, Pressure and Speed to Continuous factors; inspect main effects and estimable interactions.
Request the residual four-in-one plot and compare the fitted conclusions with the physical process question.

linear_regression.title: Linear regression
linear_regression.summary: Model a continuous response using one or more measured predictors.
linear_regression.why: You want to estimate how a numerical outcome varies with predictors or make conditional predictions. A regression provides a model for the response mean given those predictors.

setup.title: Assign outcome and predictors
setup.text: Put Yield in Dependent Variable and quantitative predictors such as Temperature and Pressure in Covariates. Put categorical predictors in Factors when present.

setup.title: Specify a meaningful model
setup.text: Choose model terms from process knowledge and the question. Interpret additive linear effects only over the observed range; a designed experiment may need the dedicated DOE analysis for its terms and coding.

setup.title: Request coefficients and diagnostics
setup.text: Request coefficient estimates and confidence intervals, model fit and residual plots. Inspect residuals versus fitted values, unusual cases and collinearity diagnostics.

setup.title: Evaluate intended use
setup.text: For prediction, evaluate performance on data not used to fit or select the model. A Bayesian Linear Regression is also available under Regression > Bayesian, with explicit prior and model choices.

columns.name: Run
columns.description: One independent process run or sampled unit.

columns.name: Yield
columns.description: Continuous yield percentage; the example stays away from 0% and 100%.

checks: Check the conditional mean pattern and residual variability. The predictors themselves do not have to be normally distributed.
Consecutive or repeated observations can have dependent errors. Use a model appropriate to their time or clustering structure.
Observational associations do not establish what will happen when a factor is deliberately changed; uncontrolled variables can confound effects.
Avoid extrapolation outside the measured operating region. A bounded percentage near 0 or 100, a binary outcome or a count may need another response model.
Generalized Linear Model does not mean arbitrary nonlinear regression. A nonlinear mechanistic equation requires a method that actually fits that equation.
report: The response, predictors, units, fitted equation and coefficient intervals.
Residual diagnostics, influential cases and dependence or sampling limitations.
For prediction, validation performance on new data and the operating range where the model is intended to be used.

example.title: Explain variation in process yield
example.story: Temperature and pressure are recorded across independent process runs. The team models how expected yield varies with those predictors over the observed operating range.
instructions: Assign Yield to Dependent Variable and Temperature and Pressure to Covariates.
Request coefficients with intervals and residual plots.
Describe the results as conditional associations unless the study design supports a causal interpretation.

related.label: These measurements come from a designed experiment

logistic_regression.title: Logistic regression
logistic_regression.summary: Model the probability of a binary outcome using process predictors.
logistic_regression.why: Your response is one of two outcomes, such as defective or not defective, and you want to account for one or more explanatory variables.

setup.title: Use one row per item
setup.text: Put Defective in Dependent Variable and set it to a nominal variable with two levels. This example records 0 for nondefective and 1 for defective.

setup.title: Assign predictors
setup.text: Move Temperature and Pressure to Covariates. Add categorical variables to Factors when relevant. Confirm which outcome level is modeled as the event.

setup.title: Interpret probabilities and odds
setup.text: Request coefficient estimates, odds ratios and confidence intervals. State the event and predictor units so an odds ratio has a clear interpretation.

setup.title: Assess fit and validation
setup.text: Inspect model diagnostics and predictive performance, especially calibration and errors relevant to the process. A Bayesian Logistic Regression is also available in Regression > Bayesian with its own prior specification.

columns.name: Temperature
columns.description: Measured process temperature in degrees Celsius.

checks: Do not apply ordinary linear regression to a binary outcome when a probability model is required.
There must be enough events and non-events for the proposed model. Sparse outcomes and complete separation can make ordinary estimates unstable or infinite.
The numerical predictors enter the log-odds model in the form you specify. Inspect whether a simple linear term is adequate.
Items from the same lot can share a failure propensity. Independence must come from the design or be represented in the model.
For aggregated failed/inspected data, use an appropriate binomial model with denominators. Do not feed percentages to the item-level binary analysis.
report: Event definition, number of events and non-events, predictors and their units.
Odds ratios with confidence intervals and predicted probabilities at relevant operating settings.
Model diagnostics, validation on new data, and limitations from rare events, clustering or confounding.

example.title: Which operating conditions predict defects?
example.story: Each component is classified as defective or nondefective, with its production temperature and pressure recorded. The model estimates how defect probability changes with those conditions.
instructions: Set Defective to Nominal and assign it to Dependent Variable.
Assign Temperature and Pressure as Covariates and verify that the modeled event is Defective = 1.
Inspect odds ratios and model diagnostics; use new data to assess prediction quality.
